en: The *Ānandamukhanirhāradharma-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying among the great nyagrodha trees at Vaiśālī. There was a monastery...
The place was named Jiaolu Zhuangjiao.
He was accompanied by a great community of bhikṣus numbering three hundred thousand.
At that time, the Buddha intended to relinquish his life-force.
He himself predicted that he would enter parinirvāṇa in three months.
At that time, the Buddha told the venerable Maudgalyāyana to go to the trichiliocosm.
He called out to all those within who were of the lineage of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
as well as those who had set forth in the Mahāyāna, commanding them all to assemble at the meeting.
Then Ma-mu-ken-lan (Maudgalyāyana) immediately received these instructions.
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, paid his respects, and departed.
By virtue of his own merit, he took a single step and trod upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.
Sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he sat down and entered into contemplation.
"What samādhi should I enter so that the sound of my invitation may be heard throughout the trichiliocosm?
At that moment, he entered the samādhi exactly as he had intended.
The sound was heard everywhere throughout the ten directions.
At that time, one million bhikṣus came to assemble at the vihāra.
The Venerable Śāriputra again gave rise to this thought:
I shall likewise, through samādhi, know the location of the bhikṣus within Jambudvīpa,
whether far or near, and cause them to assemble;
then, according to my thought, they shall all gather at the appropriate time.
He also knew the location.
At that time, four hundred thousand bhikṣus came and assembled at the vihāra.
The Buddha again addressed the bodhisattva Aprakāśalakṣaṇa.
The Bodhisattva Foremost of Confucians,
the Bodhisattva Who Abandons All Arduous Suffering,
and the Bodhisattva Who Emerges from All Darkness of Sorrow.
The Bodhisattva Remover of All Obscurations,
the Bodhisattva Sovereign Lord of All Honored Ones,
and the Bodhisattva Universal Peace of Far-Reaching Sound and Pervasive Vision.
The Bodhisattva Saṃghagandhahasta addressed the Bodhisattvas of a hundred trillion voices,
Maitreya Bodhisattva, and the others in a single word.
Go forth to the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
and call out to all therein who have resolved their minds on Bodhisattvahood—
both those who have already attained the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika) and those who have not.
Those who had already attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), as well as those who had not yet attained it,
were all made to assemble at the Crossroads Vihāra (*Saṃkrama-vihāra*).
Ten bodhisattvas each received the Buddha’s instruction, bowed their heads in reverence, and departed.
It reached everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
At that time, eight billion hundred thousand bodhisattvas who were in their last birth before buddhahood gathered there;
and one billion hundred thousand bodhisattvas who had attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) gathered there.
Three billion bodhisattvas who had attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) came to the assembly;
six billion bodhisattvas with pure resolve and liberation came to the assembly;
and those who had first conceived the great resolve and those who dwelt in accordance with the Dharma were beyond counting.
All being of one kind and sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power,
they each flew from the ten directions to arrive here;
they paid homage to the Buddha and sat together in assembly.
At that time, Śāriputra saw that the assembly of bodhisattvas,
though differing in their ranks and categories and dwelling in different places,
had all come together by flying through the air as one uniform group.
He was immediately struck with awe and fear, saying, "This must be brought about by the spiritual power and merit of the Buddha.
For what reason has such an assembly gathered?
Śāriputra then rose, adjusted his robes, and sat upright.
He prostrated before the Buddha, knelt with palms joined,
and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have a doubt and wonder that I now wish to ask of the Buddha,
so as to enable the assembly of bodhisattvas to attain direct faith."
Having heard what the Buddha taught, each attained their respective realization.
May the sutras and dharmas taught by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges cause all things to be equal.
Hearing and attaining purity,
he enables countless people to receive answers to all their various questions.
By practicing what dharma does one abide so as never to lose mindfulness?
"Will they quickly attain the unsurpassed, equal path of supreme perfect enlightenment?
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!
It is indeed for the sake of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
"To hear its meaning with such joy is indeed wonderful.
The Buddha said, "Listen attentively and hold these words well;
I shall provide you with a profound explanation."
"May all who hear this quickly attain the unsurpassed, equal path of supreme perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra, "These bodhisattvas have already attained this dharani-sūtra."
Having already illuminated all phenomena, it serves as the guide for all phenomena.
Why is this? Because it opens the way for all people.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
There are four practices by which a bodhisattva attains this Dharma. What are the four?
First, one's bodily conduct is always restrained and vigilant.
Second, that which is spoken by the mouth is always sincere;
third, that which is conceived by the mind is always gentle and compliant;
fourth, through skillful means and expedient methods, one rescues and protects all beings.
These are the four matters by which one attains this Dharma.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, there are four matters by which a bodhisattva attains the inexhaustible wisdom of the empty body."
What are the four?
First, by means of pure dwelling,
one burns away all hardships and dissipates the defilement of doubt.
First, to deliver and liberate all the people of the world;
second, to abide in purity while upholding all the teachings of the sutras to guide and benefit all;
and third, to abide in purity while upholding the merits one has performed to enrich and benefit all.
Fourth, purifying all buddha-fields and enabling all beings to transcend [suffering] so that they may attain the Buddha-dharma.
These are the four matters by which the wisdom of the pure abiding of the empty body is inexhaustible.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
Furthermore, there are four matters by which a bodhisattva maintains the *dhāraṇīmukha* and enters into birth and death,
thereby swiftly attaining [enlightenment].
What are the four?
First, through the *dhāraṇīmukha*, one quickly attains the purification of dharmas by means of worldly name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Second, through the *dhāraṇīmukha*, one enters into patience (*kṣānti*).
Third, the *dhāraṇīmukha* that fully enters the root of all thoughts and conceptions.
Fourth, the *dhāraṇīmukha* that enters all dharmas of good and evil as they are performed.
One shall swiftly attain it;
these are the four matters by which one swiftly attains this *dhāraṇīmukha*.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If a bodhisattva wishes to quickly attain the Ānanda-mukha-nirhāra-dhāraṇī,"
One should first study and understand the forty-eight names.
What are these forty-eight? The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Not being diligent in the Universal Gate (Samantamukha).
The Radiance of Illumination that Accords with the Teaching of Quiescent Extinction.
Constantly mindful of what is to be contemplated,
you are a wondrous guide.
The wondrous phrases possess mind but lack intentionality.
One whose mind is without a mind is liberated through practice.
Unshakeable by others,
there is no liberation from it.
The practice of non-arising and stainlessness is adorned with purity.
Renown is unimpeded regarding both existence and non-existence.
Regulating and stabilizing the long radiance,
one brings about their union.
Verses of Exclamation on Great Valor and Supreme Prowess.
Immovable, unmoving,
and equally moving.
Next, he dwells with firm resolve in unimpeded conduct.
The Universal Honored One diligently practices like Mount Sumeru.
Abiding in firmness and strength,
one attains great power.
Great Radiance,
Long Illumination,
Reaching All Protectors.
The Gate of Dhāraṇī Without Interruption or End, as spoken by the present Buddha, consists of these forty-eight names of divine mantras.
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
A bodhisattva should contemplate the dhāraṇī.
Thus, regarding whether a phenomenon is liberated or not liberated,
they do not form such a thought, nor do they know it, nor do they comprehend it.
Within this, there is neither increase nor decrease;
one perceives neither liberation nor non-liberation,
and one perceives neither arising nor cessation.
One does not perceive the future, the past, or the present;
one does not perceive coming nor going;
one seeks no Buddha and does not shift the mind.
Neither are they marks of physical excellence nor do they plant the seeds of such excellence;
neither are they retinues nor do they possess precepts;
neither are they samādhi nor are they wisdom.
There is neither liberation nor the wisdom that perceives liberation;
there is neither sitting nor walking, and nothing to be attained;
there is neither the removal of defilements, nor wisdom, nor the absence of wisdom.
Neither does one instruct, nor does one purify all things;
there is neither a self nor a person;
there are neither conditioned phenomena nor diligence.
It is neither practiced nor purified;
it is neither body, nor mind, nor speech;
it is neither of the future, nor of the past, nor of the present.
Nor is it for one's own person, nor for the person of another.
Thus, Śāriputra,
this Dharma is called the unsurpassed and most supreme Dharma among all dharmas.
Furthermore, to examine and collect all dharmas and to enter into all dharmas—
this is called mindfulness of the Buddha-dharmas.
This *dhāraṇī* is named "The Fierce Strategy of Dharma that Gathers All Dharmas."
This is called the Chapter on Clear Understanding and Purity, which fulfills the aspirations of all people and enables them to attain the Samādhi of Renowned Awakening.
This is called the complete realization of one's own fundamental merit.
This is called the accumulation of the seeds of the Dharma that gives rise to all the faculties of the mind,
causing one to deeply revere the marks and signs of physical perfection so adorned that no one can shake them;
even if a celestial Māra should come, he could not destroy them.
There is no one who can take it away,
and no one who can approach it. Thus, Śāriputra,
any bodhisattva who hears this Ānandamukha-nigrahītṛ-dhāraṇī...
This is for the sake of having already attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) and the unsurpassed path of equality.
Why is this? Because regarding the practices of all Buddhas, they have fully perfected them and act for the benefit of all beings.
He destroys the five realms of existence, birth, old age, sickness, death, and all doubts, fetters, and afflictions;
he swiftly attains *dhāraṇī*.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
Do not harbor the thought that dharmas are empty; Do not speak lightly of attainment or non-attainment.
Believe directly in the Dharma and do not doubt it within; Then you will swiftly attain *dhāraṇī*.
Fearing you might be bound by this emptiness, Discriminate within emptiness to attain Buddhahood swiftly.
This essential wisdom is boundless and bottomless; one swiftly attains the *dhāraṇī*.
When a bodhisattva upholds this *dhāraṇī*, it serves as the comprehensive principle for encompassing all dharmas;
thus, they hear the teachings of the Buddhas of the ten directions, and both their wisdom and all [other qualities] are fully attained.

The *Liao nihetolinni*: Just as the great radiance of the sun receives the names of all Buddhas and resolves their teachings, so too does one who purely upholds this *Mukhādhāraṇī* attain the Dharma and understand it;
whatever exists will appear before them.
Supreme among all dharmas, you protect all people in the world equally;
for the sake of humans and non-humans throughout the ten directions,
you shall explain the meaning of wisdom they inquire about during an entire kalpa and resolve all their doubts, such that your knowledge remains inexhaustible even when that kalpa has ended.
If one receives faith in the path of the sutras, And with diligence upholds the Middle Way and draws near to the True Dharma,
In one lifetime they shall be reborn in that place, And immediately become a Prince of the Dharma.
If one upholds this dhāraṇī, Then one will bring compassion to all people.
Their fame shall pervade Jambudvīpa, and they shall be praised by the World-Honored One.
Those who uphold this sutra, at the time of their death,
shall all behold eight billion koṭis of Buddhas, who will extend their hands and grant them rebirth in the honored realms.
One who possesses this *dhāraṇī* of the learner shall have all the evil,
dark, and deluded deeds committed throughout billions of *kalpas* extinguished within a single month;
if a Bodhisattva acts as a field of merit, they shall remain untiring for ten billion *kalpas*.

It is better to study *dhāraṇī*; within one month, having attained stability and fully received the exposition of *dhāraṇī*, one will completely attain all *samādhis* and wisdom, and having attained mastery of the mind, it shall no longer regress;
one shall surely attain Buddhahood with a land of one's own.
Should there be those who make offerings to this sutra,
and the Māras of the three realms attempt to disturb or destroy their resolve through demonic deeds, they will ultimately be unable to shake them;
for these people have thoroughly realized that all things are empty, and by means of this, they give birth to countless Buddhas.
These words are indeed without deviation; this *dhāraṇī* is inexhaustible.
Having heard these matters in this place, Tiṣya bestowed upon me the prediction that I would become Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; at that very moment, I saw them all.
Reverently uphold this sutra scroll; all vows shall be swiftly fulfilled.

One will enter the dharmas of the Buddha-lands, and according to what is appropriate, one will be able to transform and deliver beings, constantly purifying the Buddha-lands and remaining without blemish among the Sangha.
Questioning the profound, mysterious, and wondrous Dharma, This sutra volume can fully know that all lewdness has been eliminated;
Regarding contemplation, there are the seven factors of enlightenment, And the recollection of the eighty Buddhas and others;
All dhāraṇīs are fully maintained and bestowed.
Always keep the mind still and do not think of what is improper;
you should not think of it, and be careful not to think of it—thus thinking, do not fail to think [of this]. Later, you will attain immeasurable virtue;
you should always understand the matters of this sutra and be careful not to harbor any doubt.
Just as when a person enters the great ocean, they never say that the jewels are difficult to obtain;
so too, one who receives the bliss of gods and humans through merit will not find this matter far off, but shall swiftly attain Buddhahood.
For this reason, maintain mindfulness and do not let it depart.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"There are four practices by which a bodhisattva swiftly attains the dharma of dhāraṇī.
What are these four?"
First, to remain far removed from worldly desires;
second, not to speak of the long and short of others so that they may find no opportunity for offense;
third, when there is something requested, not to oppose the wishes of others.
Having nothing for which one feels attachment or regret later;
and fourth, practicing with diligence day and night, always intent on seeking all dharmas.
These are the four matters.
Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva practices in this way,
they will swiftly attain dhāraṇī.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
Keeping far from all evils and detached from sensual desire, one commits no sinful deeds and thus does not fall into hell;
free from the calamities of the three poisons, one abandons what is loved and attains this sutra.
Without envy toward others, one does not deceive one's own kin.
Always maintaining an equanimous mind toward all,
one should constantly renounce the body’s pleasures;
being without anger or strife in the world and not engaging in worldly affairs, one will soon attain the *dhāraṇī*.
Always studying with diligence day and night, having no expectations for external paths, and constantly seeking this supreme Dharma—then the *dhāraṇī* will manifest spontaneously.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: [This is so.]
There are four practices by which a bodhisattva swiftly attains this dhāraṇī.
What are these four?
First, dwelling alone in a secluded place;
second, abiding in the profound patience of the Dharma;
third, not feeling joy when receiving gifts.
Fourth, they do not cherish their own bodies or lives, much less their wealth and treasures.
These are the four matters.
Śāriputra, the bodhisattva practices these.
Having attained dharani,
the Buddha then spoke these verses:
"Abiding in seclusion, one contemplates the True Dharma, And does not treat others with contempt."
Birth and death burn like a blazing fire; having obtained a human body, one should practice and always maintain the mind upon profound patience.
Regarding wealth, be content with what is sufficient;
while seated within the noble assembly, give rise to an impartial mind and do not show partiality toward your own kin.
Merely by making offerings to the Buddha and the Dharma, Abiding in the power of goodness, one transcends worldly hardships;
Immediately upon shaving the hair and beard, One attains virtue and enters the subtle and wondrous.
One should know that both emptiness and worldly affairs Are thus abandoned along with all possessions.
The foolish practitioner covets wealth and profit, lacking precepts, patience, and wisdom.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, there are four practices of a bodhisattva."
One attains this dhāraṇī.
What are the four?
First, there are eight categories of syllables.
Entering into the opening of wisdom and discernment.
What are the eight?
The first is called *pā*.
By means of all phenomena of attachment, one causes them to enter into the dharma of emptiness;
these two are called "La.
Whether the Tathāgata manifests the primary and secondary marks or does not manifest the primary and secondary marks.
To enter into all phenomena with the body—
this third [syllable] is called *ba*.
Whether it be deluded phenomena or wise phenomena.
To cause others to enter into and understand the Dharma of wisdom is the fourth, named Ka.
To know all calamities and transgressions so as to enable others to enter into merit and blessings is [the fifth].
The fifth is named Ja;
knowing birth, old age, sickness, and death, one immediately enters therein into the formless realm.
The sixth is named Ta.
To view all the worlds of the various stages as empty, without being startled or alarmed, and to enter into wishlessness—
this is called the seventh, "Equanimity" (śamatha),
which brings all phenomena to rest and causes them to enter the state of the cooling Dharma.
The eighth is called "prong.
To know that all dharmas are empty is the eighth.
Furthermore, there are four matters.
First, one should constantly contemplate the eight characters.
Second, if one writes this sutra, one should write it with careful attention.
Third, if one upholds this sutra, one should uphold it with careful attention.
Recite this with sincere mindfulness until the fifteenth day.
Fourth, one should practice according to the Dharma while recollecting the eight characters.
These are the four matters.
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva should apply themselves to this practice;
they will swiftly attain dharanī.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
One should always keep in mind these eight characters; Transcribe, uphold, and reverently practice this scroll.
Read it on the fifteenth day and never depart from it; Exhort all beings to seek the path of the Buddha.
One must learn to transform and guide others; Thus one shall swiftly attain wisdom and draw near to Buddhahood.
He perceives all the Buddhas of the ten directions, as if they were all standing before him.
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, there are four things for a bodhisattva."
By recollecting the dhāraṇī, one obtains the benefits of the Dharma.
What are these four?
First, one is constantly recollected by all the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions.
Second, in whatever they undertake, Māra cannot destroy their resolve.
Third, all karmic offenses from past lives are completely extinguished.
Fourth, they never cease to speak with utmost sincerity.
He is able to resolve all questions that are asked.
These are the four matters.
Śāriputra, these are the benefits of the bodhisattva’s attainment of the *dhāraṇī* dharma.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Constantly remembered by all Buddhas, Māra cannot find an opportunity;
The sins one has committed are immediately extinguished, And one is liberated from all doubts."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"In the past, throughout ages long ago,
there were incalculable eons."
Furthermore, for twice as many incalculable, vast, and limitless eons beyond measure,
there was at that time a Buddha in the world named Ratnasaṃbhava-guṇasampanna-rāja Tathāgata.
Having transcended the four paths and not receiving further rebirth, he attained the stability of equal enlightenment in the heavens.
He was acclaimed throughout the world as the "God among Gods.
That Buddha preached the Dharma for all beings, and none could surpass him.
At the time of his parinirvāṇa, there was a Cakravartin king named Dhṛtarāṣṭra who ruled over the four continents;
his son was named Ananda.
At the age of sixteen, when his fame was fully established,
the prince went to the place where the Buddha was and heard that Buddha preach the *Dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
Having heard it, he rejoiced and immediately attained this sūtra.
Having received it, he recited and studied it, constantly mindful of upholding it.
For seven thousand years, he practiced with such diligence that he did not sleep and never rested his side upon a mat.
For seven thousand years, he did not think of sensual desires.
For seven thousand years he did not think of wealth or treasures;
for seven thousand years he did not inquire about the affairs of others;
and for seven thousand years he always dwelt alone in one place, his mind unmoved.
At that time, they all heard ninety-nine billion incalculable Buddhas preaching the Dharma of wisdom.
Having heard it, they immediately abandoned their kingdoms and renounced their kingship to become śramaṇas for ninety-nine thousand years.
He practiced the Ānandamukha-nīhāra-dhāraṇī and further expounded it to all;
throughout his lifetime, he transformed and guided the people of the world.
He caused eight hundred million nayutas of people to all resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and attain the stage of avaivartika.
At that time, there was also the son of a householder named Candraprabha (Moon-Essence).
Within the great assembly, he heard this dhāraṇī;
having heard it, he encouraged others and assisted them in upholding it.
This merit of encouragement and assistance reaches ninety million billion buddha-fields;
by making offerings to all those Buddhas,
one establishes meritorious virtue and attains all *dhāraṇīs* within all those buddha-lands.
He immediately attained the stage of being one birth away from Buddhahood and became a flying bodhisattva.
The Buddha then spoke to the bodhisattvas:
Thereupon, during those three kalpas, he made offerings to that many Buddhas.
Once the three kalpas had passed, he was to attain the unsurpassed, equal path of supreme perfect enlightenment.
At that time, there was a son of a householder named Candraprabha.
He was none other than the Buddha Ti-ho-chieh (Dīpaṃkara).
As for the king named Dhāruṇi, whose fame was fully perfected,
he was none other than Amitābha Buddha.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"During the Bhadra-kalpa,
I have taught the dhāraṇīs to the bodhisattvas."
Those who, upon hearing this sutra, experience sympathetic joy and encourage all others to do likewise,
perform acts of giving that assist and augment merit.
Having transcended four hundred thousand kalpas,
one shall no longer undergo further toil and suffering;
hereafter, one will attain the Way and exercise mastery over one's own mind.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, after making offerings to nine million buddhas,
one shall attain the unsurpassed, equal path of supreme perfect enlightenment.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
If there is a bodhisattva who, hearing this dhāraṇī for the last time,
upholds it, encourages others to do so, and rejoices in its merit,
their virtue shall be such as this.
If there are bodhisattvas who, by virtue of their merit of joy,
shed tears and have their hair stand on end out of a heart of loving-kindness while reciting this sūtra,
they shall all attain the state of *avaivartika*.
They are led into the unsurpassed path of equanimity.
Whether they write, uphold, study, recite, or read this provisional wisdom,
Śāriputra, the merit of such persons as these is immeasurable.
It is incalculable and ineffable;
no person whatsoever is able to calculate it or reach its limit.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
If one hears this and further encourages others to do so, or writes it down, maintains it, recites, and reads it—
then all devas and humans, even if they were to calculate its merit, would be unable to know the magnitude of its blessings.
Wherever such a person is born, they will always see the Buddha and attain the realization of wisdom through the profound sutras.
Firmly upholding the Dharma, he cannot be moved; swiftly attaining clear understanding and awakening, his mind is always settled, neither increasing nor decreasing.
With true insight, he does not lose the *dhāraṇī*;
free from perceptions of form, he establishes the marks and signs of excellence. He is a hero of the world, without superior.
When the son of the elder hears this sutra, he will remember his past lives in every place of birth and shall constantly behold countless Honored Ones.
He will attain Buddhahood immediately according to his vow;
if he wishes to quickly attain Buddhahood, he shall also swiftly depart from all demons.
If one wishes to attain the hundred marks of merit, one should constantly keep this in mind; such attainment will not be long delayed.

Even if one were to fill Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with precious jewels and offer them as a gift, it would not equal the merit of one who writes and upholds this [sūtra]. No analogy can ever fully match it.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If there is a bodhisattva who maintains mindfulness and studies the dhāraṇī,
there is a mountain named Himavān."
There are eight spirits within it who constantly protect it together and open up the minds and wills of people.
What are these eight?
The first is named the Deity of Courageous Strength;
the second is named the Deity Who Illuminates the Ten Directions;
the third is named the Deity Who Brings Great Benefit.
The fourth is the deity named Great Power;
the fifth is the deity named Practice of Sincerity;
the sixth is the deity named Able to Tame the Untamable.
The seventh is named the God of Youth;
the eighth is named the God of Swift Arms.
These are the names of the eight gods.
If one who studies this sutra wishes to cause a spirit to come,
they should purify themselves by bathing, put on new clothes,
and maintain a mind of loving-kindness while walking in meditation.
Throughout all kalpas,
one should then straighten the mind and recite this dhāraṇī;
one should follow this sutra and uphold it with firm devotion.
Then they quickly attained understanding and gained wisdom.
At that time, a deity stood before them.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
Furthermore, there are eight bodhisattvas dwelling in the heavens of the desire realm who constantly and impartially protect the people and bestow upon them the Way of the sutras.
Who are these eight?
The first is named the Devaputra Illuminating the Ten Directions;
the second is named the Devaputra World-Illumining;
the third is named the Devaputra Wisdom-Light.
The fourth is named Sunlight Devaputra;
the fifth is named Superior Examination Devaputra;
the sixth is named Fulfiller of Wishes Devaputra.
The seventh is named Star King Devaputra;
the eighth is named Practice Devaputra.
These are the names of the eight devaputras.
Constantly protect the people and exhort those who recite and uphold this sutra to quickly concentrate their minds and attain *dhāraṇī*.
Those who seek this sutra should always maintain a diligent resolve.
One should practice the single dharma of the dhāraṇī of mindfulness.
One must not destroy the sutras or the precepts; one's speech must be sincere, and one's conduct must likewise be so.
One should always be filial and obedient toward all elders and seniors.
One should regard all people as no different from the Buddha.
Toward those whom one holds dear and respects, one should never harbor a disrespectful mind.
By constantly reflecting on the principle of reciprocity, one immediately attains a favorable retribution;
furthermore, one attains the eye of profound patience and gains the vision of the non-arising of all phenomena.
When the Buddha preached this sutra,
bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of thirty-two Ganges Rivers all attained dharanis and established themselves on the stage of avaivartika;
sixty billion devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Thirty-two thousand devas and humans conceived the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
Heavenly flowers rained down, and lutes and musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.
At that time, Śāriputra came forward and asked the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, what is the name of this sutra, and how should it be practiced?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"This sutra is named Ānandamukha-nīhāra-dhāraṇī;
it swiftly enables all people to attain omniscience."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra,
Śāriputra, as well as the countless bodhisattvas from the ten directions,
devas, humans, gandharvas, asuras, and those who uphold the world, [all rejoiced].
They all rejoiced, approached, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, paid their respects, and departed.
*The Ānandamukhanirhāradharma-sūtra*.
